candidate_law: hook-order declaration vs declared call order: the hook-call sequence transcribed from the template method body equals the order the abstract protocol declares; on the kernel surface it is the commuting triangle `calls ; hook_rank = call_rank`
comparison_rule: an element is one hook, spelled hook:<Name>. The conventional arm (executed Python template-method code with a spy) identifies a hook when its live trace violates the declared protocol at that hook's position, when a declared step is absent from the trace, or when a concrete class defines a hook the inherited skeleton never invokes. The kernel arm identifies a hook only when a check witness resolves to one: a violation row is a Call (or Action) row, resolved through calls[row]; a dangling hook_call cell names its Hook row. unique = kernel elements minus baseline elements. A fault with no document form is recorded as a gap, never as a detection.

entries.note: one hook, one call: ordering has no content at the floor. The conventional arm has no ordering assertion to make and the kernel's equation is trivially satisfied, so the control is vacuously killed.
parity: the spy test and the kernel name the same two hooks.
parity, and only because the document author declares a hook_call coverage cell; the row-pointwise equation alone cannot see an uncalled hook.

entries.gap: the identical document is the faithful transcription of two programs that differ only in a subclass override: one is clean, one has a hook its inherited skeleton never invokes. The kernel is silent on both; no document can record the override relation.

entries.note: probe, not a fault: the same shape of drift in a straight-line procedure with no superclass, no override and no deferred step produces the same two violations. The firing carries no template-method content.
